The Ouachita madtom (Noturus lachneri) attains a maximum total length of 10 cm [Li = 10 cm], a modest size typical of small-bodied ictalurids endemic to clear, rocky streams of the Ouachita Highlands. Field surveys indicate that individuals reach sexual maturity at a total length of 6.1 cm [Lp = 6.1 cm], at which point the corresponding wet weight has been estimated at 1.56 grams [Wwp = 1.56 grams]. This length at puberty represents approximately sixty percent of the species' ultimate length, a pattern consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment. The species is iteroparous, with reproductive events distributed across the warmer months. At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a female measuring 6.9 cm in total length produces approximately 69 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 69 offspring per year], a value derived from detailed laboratory observations of spawning frequency and clutch size under controlled thermal conditions.

Yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs measuring roughly 2.5 mm in diameter. Upon eclosion, the chorion ruptures and the prolarvae emerge with substantial yolk reserves. The wet weight at birth has been recorded at 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a mass that reflects the considerable nutrient stores allocated to each offspring. This heavy investment per egg is characteristic of species that produce relatively few, large ova, enhancing the survival prospects of newly hatched individuals in the often resource-limited interstitial habitats occupied by the larvae. The yolk-sac stage lasts for several days during which the alevin remains largely sedentary, relying entirely on endogenous nutrition. Once the yolk is fully resorbed, the onset of exogenous feeding is triggered by mouth opening and swim bladder inflation, marking a critical trophic switch.

Adult body mass data indicate that spawning females can attain an ultimate wet weight of 7.2 grams [Wwi = 7.2 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the maximum total length of 10 cm [Li = 10 cm]. This corresponds to a robust body form relative to length, a feature that aids in maintaining position in swift, gravel-bottomed riffles. Juveniles grow rapidly during their first summer, with most individuals attaining a body size sufficient for overwinter survival before the onset of cold temperatures. The species exhibits a typical teleost growth pattern, with early rapid gains in length followed by a deceleration as asymptotic size is approached. Captive-reared specimens have been used to validate these growth parameters, confirming that the length-weight relationship holds across a range of environmental conditions.

At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the annual reproductive output of approximately 69 offspring [Ri = annual reproductive output of approximately 69 offspring] places the Ouachita madtom among the more fecund members of its genus. This output is sustained over a protracted spawning season, during which females may produce multiple clutches. However, reproductive effort is modulated by both temperature and food availability; individuals held at cooler temperatures exhibit reduced spawning intervals and smaller clutch sizes. The 12 °C [T = 12 °C] thermal regime used in these experiments approximates the spring and fall conditions encountered in the species' native range, suggesting that reproductive output is closely aligned with seasonal temperature cues. Field-collected gravid females corroborate these laboratory findings, with ovarian analyses revealing oocyte development consistent with continuous batch spawning.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Ouachita madtom is 3 years [am = 3 years], determined through mark-recapture studies conducted in the Little Missouri and Caddo River drainages at a mean water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively short life expectancy is typical of small, fast-growing stream fishes that experience high rates of natural mortality. Most individuals complete their reproductive lives within two to three years, with senescence and post-reproductive mortality occurring quickly after the final spawning event. Population modeling indicates that the species relies on consistent annual recruitment to maintain stable densities, as the limited lifespan constrains the number of reproductive opportunities available to any single cohort. Conservation efforts must therefore prioritize the protection of critical spawning and nursery habitats to ensure the persistence of viable age-classes.
